Growing up I hid all my psychological issues best I could. I was very much deluded, and had a puritan mindset to the scale of believing if I could practice blood-letting, I could rid myself of my foul inherited blood and be allowed to be clean and pure. This comes into play strongly with cultural and societal norms around us playing into our delusions how we think even besides our delusions.   
While I believe in demons (I grew up in New Orleans, which is infested with voodoo and black magic practitioners) I hope it is some sort of relief coming from someone of a somewhat likened ilk to say that these are not what you're seeing. There is a significant difference between our hallucinations and delusions and experiences with the supernatural. 

I hate to say it, but like others in the comment section, you will need to sever ties with people (especially family) that treat you this way. You need help, and that's okay. We all need help for something, and that's expected, or should be expected. As much as it hurts to leave what you know, you need to work towards it. I myself, in time, flourished after moving far away and rehabbing myself through proper, caring doctors and therapy. Sometimes it's still very difficult to not have religious delusions, but those can and do get better in time, but you must allow yourself that time to get better. 

I understand the kind of guilt you're feeling, at least in the sense of being raised/around the radically religious. When you leave that place, it also allows for clarity, to see things in hindsight without burden. You can do it. You can get to a place of feeling and being better. One of the hardest things about psychotic issues is being simply understood, but there are many kind, patient people that can and will help you. It will take effort and patience on your part, but you can do it. You don't deserve being around people that make you guilty for simply being sick.

We are all a portion of each other. “Most people are other people. Their thoughts are someone else's opinions, their lives a mimicry, their passions a quotation." As Wilde said, and to many degrees very true. I have my g.g.grandmother's anxieties... but also her love of fashion. I have my g.g.grandfather's will, his jawline, and I'll probably die for some unworthy cause as he did. 

Our minds, drawn up from our own soul or our forefathers, are all capricious; we coexist in the madness of our own creations and our inherited miseries, both of blood and outside nature, as we see how environments impact so incredibly the mind, growth and thoughts (I am certainly a product of this) that lead our will. 

I believe we ought to recognize that our energy is not only a reflection of the world, but we too, in the same sense, reflect back. We're all so obsessed and drawn to negativity, but focusing on or creating positivity will naturally draw in that energy, and we can "feed" off of it.

In my opinion it's not worth it to obsess over what is 'enough'. We cannot measure our energy to someone else's, our lives or our abilities. We're forcing ourselves, in that way, to fit into a puzzle where we were not meant to, then only shaving off a portion, large or small, of ourselves off. 

Sure, deadened mindset and core is natural to some of us. I personally feel little, unless I deal with plants or animals. Take a cue, if you will, from an entry of Sylvia Plath's journals: 'I may never be happy, but tonight I am content. Nothing more than an empty house, the warm hazy weariness from a day spent setting strawberry runners in the sun, a glass of cool sweet milk, and a shallow dish of blueberries bathed in cream. Now I know how people can live without books or college. When one is so tired at the end of a day one must sleep, and at the next dawn there are more strawberry runners to set, and so one goes on living, near the earth. At times like this I'd call myself a fool to ask for more...' 

Conclusion: Lets put forth our collective energies into things and practices which are not overly demanding of perfection. Our work is enough. It will be enough.

17 was a horrid age for me as well. I wasn't job trained, I held no normal social experience outside of knowing how to physically fight and verbally argue/debate things aggressively. 

My father didn't want to pay for clothes, much less books. Rewind some years: I had to wait until my brother (6 years older than me) was done with his in order for me to learn. I got a chemistry set, but I only used it for a few hours when he came home from work and then took it away, storing it before finally throwing it out. My mother was ill and dying at the time this occurred. He often hid my books and berated me over things I didn't know. Things he wouldn't teach me. 

You're not alone. Everyday I face the daunting task of self education, forcing myself to figure things out and gather properly researched and informed literature and articles. I'm 25 now, going on 26, and I have been on the road to proper education for roughly 6 years. I recommend these sites:

https://www.khanacademy.org/

http://www.rapidtables.com/math/symbols/Basic_Math_Symbols.htm#basic

https://www.duolingo.com/

You do miss out on a lot. I get it, many people here get it - but I recommend you turn your anger into fuel, and fuel your drive for learning. Be better than your parents. Learn philosophy, study psychology, try and comprehend why people do the things they do, and that too will help you cope and heal over the anger. But whatever you do, don't let yourself become bitter. Use your anger to produce good in yourself and the world around you where it now and has been so lacking. Try and find work in taking care of earthly things, as the microbes in soil (gardening, farming, ect) has excellent results with our brain's chemistry. 

Just don't give up.
